input.strategy_title: Graduate Llama Stack to General Availability
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Llama Stack shipped as Tech Preview and adoption is strong, but enterprise
customers will not build production GenAI applications on a TP component.
Graduating to GA requires API stability commitments, a production support
posture, and closing the quality gaps that TP status currently excuses. The
full inventory of those gaps is not yet known — TP feedback is scattered across
support tickets, and no systematic GA-readiness assessment has been done.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | P0 | A GA-readiness assessment inventories the gaps between current TP quality and GA bar (API stability, upgrade paths, scale limits, error handling), producing the definitive GA scope. |
| HLR-2 | P0 | Published API surface carries a stability guarantee: versioned APIs, deprecation policy, and a tested upgrade path from the last two TP releases. |
| HLR-3 | P0 | Production support posture is in place: documented SLO targets, backport policy, and supported configuration matrix. |
| HLR-4 | P1 | Safety guardrails via TrustyAI are a supported, documented integration (not an experimental flag) for GA distributions. |
| HLR-5 | P1 | The Dashboard enables Llama Stack management by default for entitled clusters (no TP opt-in gate). |
| HLR-6 | P2 | Documentation is uplifted to GA standards, including migration notes from TP. |

## Affected Components

- Llama Stack
- TrustyAI
- Dashboard

## Out of Scope

- New Llama Stack feature development beyond GA-bar quality work
- Deprecating alternative GenAI serving paths

## Open Questions

1. The GA scope itself depends on HLR-1's assessment — until it lands, the
   size of the stability and hardening work is an estimate.

# GA-readiness assessment for Llama Stack

## Description

This epic resolves the strategy's central unknown: what separates current
Llama Stack Tech Preview quality from the General Availability bar. It produces
the definitive GA-readiness assessment — a systematic inventory of gaps across
API stability, upgrade paths, scale limits, and error handling — and derives
from it the definitive GA scope that all Llama Stack hardening work in this
strategy is sized against. The strategy notes that TP feedback is scattered
across support tickets and no systematic GA-readiness assessment has been
done; this epic is that assessment.

## Scope

- Sweep the sources of TP-era quality feedback (support tickets, issue
  trackers, release notes, known-issues records) and consolidate them into a
  single evidence base.
- Inventory the gaps between current TP quality and the GA bar, per dimension:
  - API stability (surface churn, undocumented behavior, breaking changes
    across TP releases)
  - Upgrade paths (path and friction from prior TP releases)
  - Scale limits (documented and observed limits under load)
  - Error handling (coverage, consistency, and actionability of failures)
- Classify each gap: must-fix for GA, acceptable-with-documentation, or
  deferred, with severity and the GA-bar delta stated.
- Produce the definitive GA scope: each must-fix gap mapped to the
  implementation work that remediates it (within the API-stability work, the
  support-posture work, or as recommended follow-up epics).
- State explicitly, for each finding, whether it changes the scope or approach
  of the API-stability and support-posture work, since those are sized on the
  current estimate.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A single assessment document exists that inventories gaps in all four named
  dimensions (API stability, upgrade paths, scale limits, error handling), with
  no dimension left as "unknown" without a stated reason and a follow-up
  action.
- Every inventory entry carries a classification (must-fix / document /
  defer), a severity, and the specific GA-bar criterion it fails or meets.
- The assessment's evidence base is traceable — each gap cites its source
  (ticket, test result, or measured observation).
- The assessment produces a definitive GA scope: every must-fix gap is mapped
  to the work item that remediates it, and the mapping is unambiguous about
  which existing work stream absorbs it versus which requires new work.
- Given the assessment's findings, a reviewer can determine, for each finding,
  whether the API-stability or support-posture work's scope changes — the
  assessment states this per finding.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): GA-readiness assessment inventories the gaps between current TP
  quality and GA bar, producing the definitive GA scope. This epic is that
  requirement in full.

# Llama Stack API stability guarantee and TP upgrade path

## Description

This epic delivers the API stability guarantee that GA requires for Llama
Stack: the published API surface becomes versioned, carries a deprecation
policy, and has a tested upgrade path from the last two TP releases. It also
remediates the API-stability gaps that the GA-readiness assessment identifies
as must-fix, making the published surface one the platform can commit to
supporting. The scope of hardening is sized against that assessment's
definitive GA scope — until it lands, this epic's content is an estimate and
may be rewritten, so the work starts once the assessment resolves. The
upgrade-path verification in this epic's scope is evaluated against the
supported configuration matrix that the production support-posture work
publishes, so that work lands before the verification completes.

## Scope

- Version the published API surface (the OpenAI-compatible REST APIs and the
  distribution CRD surface) so GA consumers can pin against a stable version.
- Define and publish the deprecation policy for the API surface: how breaking
  changes are signaled, how long deprecated surface remains available, and
  what consumers must migrate to.
- Build and verify the upgrade path from the last two TP releases to the GA
  release, including migration of existing distribution resources.
- Remediate the API-stability gaps classified as must-fix by the GA-readiness
  assessment (surface churn, undocumented behavior, breaking changes), or
  record an explicit deferral with rationale for each.
- Verify upgrade-path behavior across the supported configuration matrix so
  the tested upgrade path matches supported configurations.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The published API surface is versioned, and the versioning scheme is
  documented where consumers interact with it.
- A deprecation policy exists and is applied: any existing API surface that
  will change or disappear under GA is marked with its deprecation path per
  that policy.
- The upgrade path from each of the last two TP releases is exercised and
  passes: an existing TP deployment upgraded to the GA release retains its
  intended behavior, with any required migration steps documented.
- Every API-stability gap the GA-readiness assessment classified as must-fix
  is either remediated in this epic's deliverable or carries a recorded,
  justified deferral accepted by the strategy owner.
- Upgrade-path verification evidence exists per supported configuration
  matrix entry that the support-posture work publishes (each combination
  tested, or explicitly excluded from support with rationale).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0): published API surface carries a stability guarantee — versioned
  APIs, deprecation policy, and a tested upgrade path from the last two TP
  releases. This epic covers that requirement in full, including the
  assessment-driven API-stability remediation.

# Llama Stack production support posture

## Description

This epic puts the production support posture in place that Llama Stack GA
requires: documented SLO targets, a backport policy, and a supported
configuration matrix. It also remediates the scale-limit and error-handling
gaps the GA-readiness assessment classifies as must-fix, so the component is
supportable at GA rather than merely feature-complete. The scope of hardening
is sized against that assessment's definitive GA scope — until it lands, this
epic's content is an estimate and may be rewritten, so the work starts once
the assessment resolves.

## Scope

- Define and document SLO targets for the GA distribution (availability and
  operational objectives the support organization commits to).
- Define and document the backport policy: which releases receive fixes, for
  how long, and how security and critical fixes flow to supported releases.
- Define the supported configuration matrix: the provider, deployment, and
  scale configurations that are supported at GA, each validated rather than
  merely asserted.
- Validate each supported configuration matrix entry with a defined
  smoke/validation run, so "supported" means tested.
- Remediate the scale-limit and error-handling gaps classified as must-fix by
  the GA-readiness assessment, or record an explicit deferral with rationale
  for each.
- Ensure error handling on the supported surface is consistent and actionable
  (failures identify the failing resource and the remediation path) for the
  cases the assessment flags.

## Acceptance Criteria

- SLO targets are documented and stated in measurable terms, and each has an
  owner for its measurement.
- The backport policy is documented and covers every GA-supported release,
  including security and critical-fix handling.
- The supported configuration matrix is published, and every matrix entry has
  a passing validation run recorded against the GA release — entries that
  cannot be validated are explicitly excluded from support with rationale.
- Every scale-limit and error-handling gap the GA-readiness assessment
  classified as must-fix is either remediated in this epic's deliverable or
  carries a recorded, justified deferral accepted by the strategy owner.
- Documented scale limits state the observed boundary, not only the intended
  one, for the limits the assessment examined.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P0): production support posture is in place — documented SLO
  targets, backport policy, and supported configuration matrix. This epic
  covers that requirement in full, including assessment-driven scale-limit and
  error-handling remediation.

# TrustyAI guardrails as supported Llama Stack integration

## Description

This epic promotes the TrustyAI safety-guardrails integration for Llama Stack
distributions from an experimental flag to a supported, documented
integration, as GA distributions require. The integration already exists
behind an experimental opt-in; this epic makes it a first-class supported
surface: validated on GA configurations, safe in its failure modes, and
documented for users. The work spans the TrustyAI operator/integration side
and the Llama Stack distribution configuration that consumes it; the TrustyAI
team owns the integration's support posture.

## Scope

- Remove the experimental gating so the TrustyAI guardrails integration is a
  supported configuration for GA Llama Stack distributions (not an
  experimental flag).
- Validate the integration end-to-end on a GA-configuration distribution:
  guardrails requests flow between the Llama Stack distribution and the
  TrustyAI service and are enforced as configured. Here a GA-configuration
  distribution means one deployed with the GA release's supported provider
  and deployment configuration (the distribution CRD's supported surface for
  that release) — a property of the release under validation, defined
  independently of the enumerated supported configuration matrix that the
  production support-posture work publishes in parallel.
- Define and validate fail-mode behavior: what happens to requests and to the
  distribution when the guardrails provider is unavailable or misconfigured,
  with the degradation explicit rather than emergent.
- Document the supported integration: supported configuration, setup, and
  behavior, including the fail-mode behavior above, as user-facing
  documentation for the integration.
- Confirm the supported designation with the support posture it implies
  (where users report issues, what is covered).

## Acceptance Criteria

- On a GA-configuration Llama Stack distribution with TrustyAI deployed, the
  guardrails integration works without any experimental opt-in flag, and a
  request subject to a configured guardrail is handled per that guardrail.
- Fail-mode behavior is defined, implemented, and verified: with the
  guardrails provider unavailable, the distribution behaves per the documented
  policy (e.g., fail closed or open per configuration) — not with an undefined
  error.
- The integration is documented end-to-end (configuration, setup, behavior,
  fail-mode), and the documentation matches the validated behavior.
- The experimental flag (or its equivalent gating) is removed or retired such
  that no user action is required to reach the supported configuration.
- Misconfiguration produces an actionable error identifying the misconfigured
  resource.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-4 (P1): safety guardrails via TrustyAI are a supported, documented
  integration (not an experimental flag) for GA distributions. This epic
  covers that requirement in full.

# Dashboard Llama Stack management enabled by default

## Description

This epic makes the Dashboard's Llama Stack management capability available by
default for entitled clusters, removing the Tech Preview opt-in gate. Today
users must opt in to see Llama Stack management in the Dashboard; at GA the
capability is simply present for entitled clusters. Because this changes
default user-facing behavior, it ships with a rollback path.

## Scope

- Enable the Llama Stack management sections (navigation, resource views, and
  management surfaces for Llama Stack distributions) by default for entitled
  clusters, removing the TP opt-in gate from the user path.
- Define and implement the non-entitled behavior: clusters without the
  relevant entitlement do not get the capability surfaced (or see the defined
  not-entitled state), matching entitlement behavior for other GA
  capabilities.
- Retain a configuration-level rollback: administrators can disable Llama
  Stack management via the Dashboard's configuration surface, so the
  default-on change is reversible without a code rollback.
- Update any captions, labels, or TP designations on the Llama Stack
  management surfaces that fall out of this change (GA designation replaces TP
  designations).

## Acceptance Criteria

- On an entitled cluster with a Llama Stack distribution present, a user sees
  Llama Stack management in the Dashboard with no opt-in action.
- On a cluster without the relevant entitlement, Llama Stack management is
  not enabled by default, and the behavior matches the defined
  non-entitled state.
- No TP opt-in gate remains in the user path for Llama Stack management.
- Rollback: an administrator can disable Llama Stack management via
  configuration, and the Dashboard reflects the disabled state — verified as a
  pass/fail check, since this change replaces the existing opt-in behavior.
- No stale TP-labeled captions or designations remain on the Llama Stack
  management surfaces.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-5 (P1): the Dashboard enables Llama Stack management by default for
  entitled clusters (no TP opt-in gate). This epic covers that requirement in
  full.

the GA feature set that the implementation work in this strategy actually
delivers — the versioned API surface and deprecation policy, the support

  changes, aligned with the tested upgrade path.
